sections.heading: Daisugi Testnet Status and Roadmap
sections.summary: Testnet v0.1 (ERC-4337) and v0.2 (adds native frame transactions) are live; v0.3 targeting EIP-8288 mempool aggregation is next.
sections.body:
Antonio Sanso opened with no formal agenda — the call was given over to the Daisugi testnet (daisugi.fyi) and a request for implementation help.
Credits for the testnet: Giulio, Riva Labs, Emil, and the EF DevOps team.
Version 0.1 used non-native account abstraction (ERC-4337) with a SPHINCS variant for signatures.
Version 0.2 is already deployed and lets a user choose per transaction between ERC-4337 (non-native) and frame transactions (EIP-8141, native).
  - The testnet runs Nethermind, using its frame-transaction implementation.
Version 0.3 is the next target: in-mempool signature aggregation per EIP-8288.
  - Repeatedly described as "virgin territory" — nobody has implemented EIP-8288 yet, and the call was an open call for collaborators.
Emil has already produced a LeanVM fork parameterized to match the Lean SPHINCS parameters shipped on the testnet, with patches from Riva Labs.
Anyone wanting to help with v0.3 can ask Antonio to be added to the testnet Telegram group.

sections.heading: Aggregation Architecture and Block Building
sections.summary: An aggregator strips per-transaction signatures and replaces them with one constant-size aggregated proof built by LeanVM, keeping block size flat as transaction count grows.
sections.body:
Antonio diagrammed the target flow on a shared [Excalidraw whiteboard](https://excalidraw.com/#room=ce6509e21555e3b01536,JFWJxcjbbM2vWqBOfBQblg).
Naive path: each user submits (transaction, signature) to the mempool and the builder puts both in the block — with post-quantum signatures this blows up block size.
EIP-8288 path introduces an aggregator role, which for the first version is also the block builder:
  - The aggregator takes T1, T2, … from the mempool and produces a single aggregated signature, SA, using LeanVM.
  - The block then carries T1 and T2 without their signatures, plus SA.
  - SA is constant size — it does not matter whether the block holds 10, 100 or 200 transactions, so per-signature size stops mattering.
LeanVM's aggregation uses Flock, with WHIR for wrapping up the proof; the code is in the LeanVM repository.
  - Wrapped proof size is roughly 200 KB.
  - Matteo Vicari put early aggregation throughput at about 20 signatures per second on a regular machine, and stressed the figure is preliminary.
Verification side: rather than a precompile, each client would embed LeanVM and call its verification when validating a block.
  - At the moment the testnet's Nethermind does ECDSA verification; the plan is to fork it so verification also checks the LeanVM proof.
Gottfried Herold endorsed starting with the easier, non-recursive case first.

sections.heading: ethrex In-Mempool Aggregation Prototype
sections.summary: LambdaClass shared an ethrex branch prototyping in-mempool aggregation with LeanVM, plus benchmarks; it covers validation and mempool aggregation.
sections.body:
Tomás Grüner shared an [ethrex branch for EIP-8288](https://github.com/lambdaclass/ethrex/tree/eip-8288) implementing in-mempool aggregation with LeanVM.
[Benchmarks for it](https://github.com/lambdaclass/ethrex/commit/b5c3a098ce8041c8e38b7ebe22eed83c400ef35c) were posted in chat.
The prototype covers block validation, and mempool aggregation was in progress.
Asked in chat whether recursive aggregation is supported, Tomás answered yes.
Antonio confirmed the plan is to start without recursive aggregation and get an end-to-end version working first:
  - "As long as we have a first version of EIP-8288, and then any form of validation with ethrex or Nethermind, we are happy, and then we can be more crazy."

sections.heading: Reading EIP-8288: Dependency Frames and Test Case 7
sections.summary: Antonio walked through EIP-8288's dependency triples and test case 7; several details of the spec text remained unclear to everyone present.
sections.body:
The group is targeting EIP-8288 test case 7 (recursive mempool aggregation), which is effectively a wrapper around test case 1.
Test case 1 is a transaction with a single dep verify frame mode frame carrying one (LEANSPHINCS_SCHEME, msghash, pubkey_hash) triple, followed by a VERIFY frame.
Stefano De Angelis summarized the triple in chat, which Antonio read out:
  - LEANSPHINCS_SCHEME identifies the signature scheme to use.
  - msghash is the hash of the transaction or message being authorized.
  - pubkey_hash identifies the public key expected to verify that signature.
  - The dependency is then checked in the VERIFY frame.
Matteo Vicari said Riva Labs only started looking at this the day before, and is working through the account abstraction path first because it is easier to reason about.
  - Open items on their side: cross-verification by other nodes, and the rejection path when aggregation fails.
Both Antonio and Matteo said the spec text is hard to decode, particularly how the witness links the aggregation proof to each transaction's message.
Antonio proposed inviting the EIP authors (Vitalik and Tomas) to a future call to resolve the remaining questions.

sections.heading: Performance and Sizing Side Questions
sections.summary: Preliminary numbers: ~20 aggregated signatures per second with testnet parameters versus ~280 upstream; a few hundred signatures per block is the practical target.
sections.body:
Stefano asked how many signatures would realistically be aggregated in a block.
  - Antonio: a few hundred, less than a thousand — anchored on current mainnet transactions per block.
Aggregation throughput, all described as preliminary and expected to improve substantially:
  - Upstream Lean SPHINCS parameters: about 280 signatures per second.
  - The forked version matching the testnet parameters: about 20 per second.
Matteo noted throughput depends on the SPHINCS parameters, the hardware, and the hash function, since Flock performs differently across them.
Stefano gave reference points from WOTS, which he knows by heart: Flock proving is around 200 ms for a few hundred signatures, and about a second for a thousand.
  - Benedikt Wagner noted recent one-time-signature work where Justin claimed roughly a 4X improvement.
  - Antonio recalled a target of 8,000 to 16,000 signatures for WOTS.
Stefano's rough hash-function ratios: a factor of about 2 between Blake3 and SHA, and another factor of about 2 between SHA and Keccak.
Matteo emphasized the bottleneck is proof creation, not verification.

sections.heading: Dependency/Wrapper Decoupling and Native Verification
sections.summary: The VERIFY frame checks only the dependency; verifying the aggregated proof needs native client support, since on-chain WHIR verification would cost far too much gas.
sections.body:
Stefano De Angelis (Nethermind) walked the group through his reading on the whiteboard:
  - The dependency describes the object being authenticated and how it is authenticated; the VERIFY frame only checks that the dependency is valid.
  - The public key in the triple is the sender's — the authorizer's — not the aggregator's.
  - The wrapper object is broadcast at the network level and is not accessible from inside the frame. It carries a reference to the dependency plus the actual signature.
  - The aggregator checks that the wrapper holds the correct signature for the dependency the frame verified, then proves that verification.
  - He described the aggregating party as a prover: it first verifies the Lean SPHINCS signatures, then proves that the verification was valid.
Antonio's open question: with the frame only verifying the dependency, how does a receiving node verify the aggregated proof itself?
  - Doing it in a smart contract means verifying a WHIR proof on chain, which Matteo said would take an enormous amount of gas.
  - Antonio is not interested in the on-chain route; he wants a Nethermind fork that verifies natively, the way ECDSA is verified today.
Stefano De Angelis agreed native in-client verification is the direction, but said it does not exist yet and that this is his own reading rather than a settled design.
Aggregation cadence: Stefano De Angelis noted the spec aggregates on a short interval rather than only at block-building time; Antonio said v0.3 will aggregate once and keep it simple.
The missing piece both identified: something that links the frame to the witness so a client can conclude the signature was verified and move on to executing the user's frame.

sections.heading: Nethermind Joining the Testnet Effort
sections.summary: Stefano De Angelis (Nethermind) joined the testnet effort and will bring a concrete test case 7 proposal to the next call.
sections.body:
Antonio invited anyone interested in v0.3 to join the testnet Telegram group; Stefano De Angelis asked to be added.
Nethermind has been implementing frame transactions and is scoping EIP-8288 integration as the next step in the client.
Stefano De Angelis offered to bring a concrete solution to the verification problem to the next call, with test case 7 as the objective.
Antonio will try to bring in the EIP-8288 authors, Vitalik and Tomas, to a future call.
The [LeanVM repository](https://github.com/leanEthereum/leanVM) was shared in chat.
Next call in two weeks.
